p: I would say that— so it's reasonable to assume, like, I have the USTA in my district.
Yes.
Traffic man— traffic management is a major issue at that one event.
Yes.

Now we have events that are 10 times that size. Have we hired additional indivi— like, how are we going to be equipped? Saying we're going to keep everyone safe is

great, but how are we going to physically do that if we don't have additional resources to take on what's about to come?
Well, I can't comment on that with regard to PD resources.
Okay.

That would need to be spoken to by the NYPD. If we're talking about those individual events, like the fan engagements, from a resource management of like volunteers that are going to be helping with crowd control, et cetera, then those entities and organizations do have their own plans in place and have hired their own staff. And then we're also working with volunteers through different programs to ensure that we have people there to help direct people to, you know, whether it be metro stations or otherwise positioned in and around those fan zones, like the ones at Rock Center, like the ones at USTA. So that's how we're managing it from that standpoint, a non-security standpoint.

And just to consider, and it's not just NYPD, it's Sanitation, it's all the agencies that are going to have to deal

with this. But moving on, because we talked about Fan Fest, have we looked into a transportation plan? Again, the last time you guys were here, I mentioned the seven train on a good day is packed to capacity. Will there be a ferry service in operation? Will the LIRR be available?

Thank you. We are working with the MTA to ensure that any of these locations that have high influx, like we would for any event that happens in those locations. For example, the US Tennis Center, when we have all– whether it be a concert or anything else going on in that area, we work directly with the MTA to ensure that there's increased service on those lines to accommodate the influx of individuals coming into the area. Also work with organizations like TLC with regard to rideshare. So all of that is in planning and in the works to ensure that we are not over-impacting that neighborhood with a number— an exorbitant number of people that don't have anywhere to go.
One more question from the council member?

Yes, thank you. Going back to the permits for businesses to participate, have you all— it's kind of a two-part question— have you all thought about a more equitable fee structure that would enable smaller businesses? I'm talking about businesses that have a smaller capacity, can maybe seat 99 people or less, so they can participate in a meaningful way. And also, given the application deadline, we've already kind of entered into the far end for both plaza events, streets events. Is it– realistically, how many additional permits do you think you'll be able to give out from this point on?

Well, honestly, our deadline, our shortest deadline, I think, 30 days. So we're still accepting applications as it stands. All those applications are in process and being reviewed. There are all the agencies that you mentioned before, like Sanitation, Health Department, all of them play a part in processing those applications. So they are under review. It is not our policy to give away that type or issue that type of permit this far in advance. So we are still in process reviewing all of the asks with regard to

the costs associated with it. These are our administrative fees, so they are– they are set for the city standpoint with regard to the amount of time and energy it takes to process those applications.

And I was just— the comment, my only fear is because the permit process takes so long that businesses or that are just really hearing about what's going on, do we think it's really enough time for them to apply?
Again, our street events, even that for a full street closure is 30 to 45 days. So if they were to apply now, we could still review the application.
Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, Council Member. Just turning– turning to the fan zones, since those did, did just come up, how were those five sites selected? Was there a competitive process, or were community boards or local officials consulted in the selection of the sites?

Thank you, Chair. The five fan festivals were– those locations were chosen by the host committee prior to this

administration and prior to my sitting in this position. So I cannot speak to the process, but yeah, I'll end there.
Thank you. Do we know if the contracts for the fan zones have local hiring commitments, and if you can speak to that?

Thank you. Each Fan Fest site is a bit different in terms of how hiring is managed. For example, the Rockefeller Center site is managed by Tishman Speyer [sp?], similar to Christmas tree lightings. My team, in coordination with the Mayor's Office on Labor is in conversations with the host committee, CLC, and others to ensure that wherever possible, local hires are made and union labor is utilized.

Great. And on the point about the moratorium from BIDs, if you can specifically speak to that when we're promoting city-run fan zones while simultaneously preventing other organizations from hosting programming, whether or not it's related to the Cup?

Thank you. There's actually not been a moratorium. I understand that that's been out there. There is no moratorium on

applications. The— we have met even since last year in October with the BIDs and event organizers to ensure that they understand how to apply for events during this time period and continue to meet with them. BIDs have put in applications for the types of activities that they would like to hold in these spaces, and all those applications, as I mentioned before, are under review. There is a timeframe that we are not accepting applications only for plaza locations, and that is June— sorry, July 3rd through July 8th, because that corresponds when we have the International Labor Review, 4th of July, all of that stuff. So we can't actually add additional events on top of that. And SAPO has put out our— I should say ECM SAPO has also put out our embargo for the FIFA World Cup on our website, which clearly outlines the dates, times, and locations that are not available for permitting in New York City during the timeframe of the World Cup spanning June 11th to July 19th.
Would you say typically summer programming is approved and clear by this timing?
Absolutely. By now? No.
Like by– by like end of April that some of the permits would've–
[interposing] No.
been already approved?

Absolutely not. The– I would say that maybe they might be approved seven days in advance. That is our standard. It does– we have a deadline for a reason, 30 days in advance. It does take that entire time to get everything on board. Even something as simple as a street festival requires a lot of resources and agency coordination to get it in place. And there are a lot of support permits that are required by the individual organizers putting on the events and then city, state, and federal regulations that have to be adhered to. So it does take time to work with these organizers to ensure that they are setting up an event that is safe for everyone to attend, and so they wouldn't be receiving an application— or sorry, a permit— this far out in advance of that activity.
So you're saying that events usually don't get approved till seven days before?
That is correct. Issue the permit? Yes.
Alright. Council Member Farias?

Thank you, Chair. The administration has emphasized that every borough is going to be included in FIFA fan activations, but, you know, inclusion alone is sometimes not equity. I want to understand whether the Bronx is receiving comparable investment, visibility, and economic opportunity throughout the time frame where we're hosting FIFA. Can you folks break down the total public and private investment per borough fan zone, if we have that available at this time frame? Any capital investments, programmatic, security, marketing costs, things like that?
Thank you, Council Member. That's not information that I have available right now, but we're happy to get back to your office.
Okay. So, there is— there is like a— you folks are looking at a makeup of minimum investment thresholds per borough, or are most of the allocations discretionary?
Regarding which allocation specifically?
Towards the fan zone planning and programming.

I can share that the dates for the fan zones were announced yesterday. They were dependent, I would say, based on the suitability of the location. So USTA and Brooklyn Bridge Park have the longest activation periods. Again, those decisions were made by the host committee and were well underway when we came in in February. We did make sure that there is at least one of the official zones in each borough, but the length of those do vary.

Yeah, I mean, the Bronx, at least from what I've seen in the announcement, unless something has changed in 24 hours or so, only have two days of activation at the beginning of the FIFA timeline. And so with over 45 days– I think it's 47 in total– I'm just wondering

how that's equitable towards the Bronx. I understand in hearing your response that that was prior to you here, but these things are still in development, or at least can be, and I'm just wondering what that looks like in terms of equity or economic opportunity for a borough that, I might add, is on mainland and has access to a lot of people both out of our five boroughs, like what that looks like for the Bronx.

Thank you, Council Member. The fan zones themselves are something we will certainly continue to work with the host committee on and hear you loud and clear. I think what's great about some of the programming that we're talking about today is it, you know, it's not just that host committee programming, and so that is where we will be working and announcing more programming to come that I think is a bit more equally divided among boroughs. And in addition to making sure that cultural institutions, parks, others are plugged into these promotional opportunities that, you know, a lot of the programming that I know NYC Tourism is working on and that we're very excited about is really encouraging New Yorkers to visit a borough they maybe haven't been to or haven't been to

in a while, you know, to go eat Ecuadorian food when Ecuador is playing, things like that. So that really is a focus of our team. And I know NYC Tourism echoes that, is highlighting those opportunities across the boroughs and encouraging not just tourists, but New Yorkers to use this as a time to go visit a different neighborhood.

Okay. I'd love to keep the conversation going with you folks, especially on my borough. We have a lot of diversity, a lot of different eateries, folks that actually participate in Restaurant Week and such. We've worked together on that in the past, and I'd love to see opportunities come not only for just vendors and like for the workforce itself, but also for a fan activation and trying to get more folks than just, you know, people in the city or Bronxites into a fan space. So, thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you. I want to go back to the Cultural Passport and better understand some of the venues that are going to be included. Will it include live music venues, small theaters, comedy clubs?
Yes, that is my understanding. That would be available to all of those entities, and then the New York City Tourism Portal would be as well.

And do we have a sense of equity by borough, like how many cultural institutions have signed up already from each borough? And do we need a targeted outreach plan to get more cultural institutions on board?

Thank you, Chair. The sign-up for that has not opened yet, so we don't have a number yet, but we will certainly keep an eye towards that as we look at the signups coming in, and I know doing very comprehensive outreach is part of the planning.
And when do you expect that to begin?
I don't have that in front of me. We're just confirming the contract and exactly what everything looks like, but we can get back to your office with that.
And will organizations need to specify accessibility features that each institution has– we can have that flag?

Thank you, Chair. For— I can't– unfortunately, I don't know that information for the passport. I can tell you that some of the other opportunities, you know, we're making sure that the ability to sort by accessibility or choose specifically accessible options is part of the interface.
And do we know what other safeguards might be in place to help ensure equity across boroughs and not being overly concentrated in already major tourist areas?

I'm confident that we will at minimum meet the stipulations put forth in the legislation to have five in each borough. So those safeguards that are in place, I committed to ensuring that our cultural passport meets those, and we'll be working closely with Team Wonder and our partner agencies in making sure that outreach has been proportionate and that sign-ups are proportionate as well.

Do we have a sense of what the success metrics will be for participation or broader engagement or economic impact in the

communities that, you know, we're driving additional traffic to?

Appreciate that question, Chair. I think for initial success metrics will be that number of signups and seeing that it is– you know, represents the institutions that are possible and available in each borough to sign up. And with the various contacts between DCLA, SBS, and others, again, I think we'll have a good sense of, you know, we know who's missing and we'll make sure that they do sign up and are part of it. We're in conversation with EDC and others about success as a whole and what that economic impact looks like and can certainly incorporate the passport into that.
On the calendar and the map, which designated agency is going to be responsible for maintaining it?
That is us, NYC Tourism.
And how will coordination across all the different players and the agencies be managed?

We have been working with all of our BID and chamber partners, as well as folks like that New York City Hospitality Alliance, and other dining out program. We want to make sure that it is very deep and broad in terms of participation. So we have been doing quite a bit of proactive outreach. There was a webinar a couple of weeks ago that was given by the host committee and Google for the AI tool, the navigation tool, and all of our systems on the backend will speak to each other. So if you are participating in our program, if you submit an offer or an event to our calendar, that will surface in the tool. So we had, I think, about 1,100 businesses join that, because the first order of business is to make sure your Google business profile is populated and accurate and up to date. So we're seeing the interest. We of course are going to our members as well, but we're trying to go as broadly as we can. We welcome any additional outreach. Since it began opening, I would say two weeks, we are at about 71 events so far as of this morning. But we're expecting more of that to heat up as we get closer. So we're always interested in more support for outreach, but

we're actively doing that. We have another webinar that we're planning in about a week or two to remind.
Events are, uh, constantly updating with like location, date, and time. So how will you, to make sure it's up to date in real time?

The event itself will be submitting on their own behalf. And then we will take that and there will be a couple of human beings on our side who will go and check it, make sure there's a photo attached, make sure that the dates are accurate. And if something should change on the event side, we would hope that that organization would update. If anything, we might not be in a position to know if their event is changing, because we are not managing the events–
[interposing] Right, right.
but we will be checking to make sure that there's accuracy and the information is complete and it will be refreshed. We're going to be taking submissions until July 1.
And what systems or tools are you using to collect all that information?
We are building it.
Okay.

So we have developers. We did this in a similar way for the 400th last year. This is just an expanded tool, because we're going way beyond and we want to make sure the capacity is much broader. So yeah, our internal development team will be doing that.
And is this something that would be replicable in the future or technology could continue to use?

Absolutely. We always are refining our site and integrating more efficiencies with regard to AI to make sure that our site is a source of truth, whether our consumer is going to ChatGPT or they're coming to our site. So we're always making sure our information is accurate, period. Otherwise, we won't be recognized as that authoritative source. So we, again, it's great to have the machines, but the human beings are the ones checking to make sure that if

we're not accurate, we might not surface. And we know folks are not always coming to our channels, even on an organic basis. But when we put paid media behind it, then they do. So as an ongoing effort, we make sure that we're refreshing and maintaining accuracy so we can surface everywhere our consumer's going.
And a similar question is, how will you measure success of the— of these initiatives?

Across the board for everything we're doing, it's participation. We also have a tool that we've added through Tourism Economics, which is a division of Oxford Economics, where we will be able to see if someone came to our website and then visited a borough. And there are a number of points of interest across the boroughs. So post-World Cup, we'll be able to look to see if we move the needle on those visitation. And we'll be able to understand exactly what they did. Did they come to the site? Did they look at the calendar and then they visited? So I think it's participation in the programs, and then did we actually drive people and move them?
Glad to hear that you're tracking that data and looking forward to seeing the results–
[interposing] Thank you.
of what we can deliver here. On the cultural maps, how are you defining a cultural corridor?

So the navigation tool, we're– you know, our AI visitor concierge is going to be coordinated with the events calendar and the other programs that we are doing. So the AI tool is also serving as the map. It's powered by Google Maps. So when you search for something and you pull up a neighborhood, you will see the businesses that will surface. And that is scraping from our website, New Jersey Transit's site, Port Authority. We'll have live inputs, and the host committee site. So assuming you have your Google business profile active, you will surface. And if you're participating in our programs, that will come up as well. So we have the $26 and the Cup program. If you're— if you submitted an event to the calendar, all of that will come up. And so it's a sort of a

combination of live navigation based on all the inputs we're getting, mapping, and coordination with the calendar. So on the back end, everything is speaking to each other, and those tools will work together.
And today, if I wanted to see a complete list of the World Cup events and fan activities, where would it— where would I go?

The calendar won't be live until the end of May. We're still collecting. What you will see on our site are roundups. So we have content that will indicate where to watch if you're, you know, a fan of a particular team. We are also building team landing pages. So we'll drive folks directly there. If you're a fan of France, you can go there and find out all the places to watch. So there's a lot of content up there now. It's not in calendar form yet, but there's quite a bit of neighborhood guides and such fan guides that are available now on nycitourism.com.

And how will the NYC Tourism website versus the host committee website, how will those two play together? In the press conference yesterday, the administration was

directing people to the host committee's website. So just curious what the vision is.

We are partnering different information. The host committee is the authority on transportation, all things MetLife Stadium tickets, all that, obviously through FIFA. We are linking to their site pretty prominently from ours. We are more about the disbursement and the neighborhoods, and we are using the fan zones as anchor points. So when someone goes to Queens, for example, we're showing them everywhere else to go while they're there. That's not content that the host committee will cover. So we're doing all of that and we're trying to create a pretty integrated ecosystem. So– and making it very clear to the consumer where to go– which site to go to based on the information you're looking for. So they're much on the line of logistics, game details, et cetera. And we are more in the name of small business and local borough disbursement. And we're linking to each other.
I want to invite Council Member Thomas-Henry to ask a few more questions.
That confused me a little bit. What– what's linking to one another with the sites and the small borough? Yeah, yeah.

Yeah, there's going to be– there is currently two different websites, the host committee site and ours. We're covering all the content around what to do while you're here using the fan zones and the matches as anchor points. So if you want to go to the fan zone in Queens, we're going to tell you what else to do while you're there. So itineraries, neighborhood guides, watch parties, all of that content will only be on our site. The host committee site is very much more about the games, tickets, transportation, all of the logistical detail to get to and from. We are linking to each other's sites. So it's different information and we're trying not to step on each other with, you know, the same information.
So by your site, is the nycitourism.com site?
Yes. Yes.

Okay, perfect. So, I wanted to ask specifically about that, like when you look at your team section and it kind of goes by the different teams and one is Celebrate Ecuador. Are these businesses— the businesses that are being promoted now, are these paid ads, or is the idea to get more local businesses up here?

We do not charge to appear on our website, and we do not relegate only to our member base, especially for the World Cup. So no, we have a team that actively researches and works with local businesses and our BIDs and chambers to understand what businesses we should be featuring, what's relevant to the topic at hand. No, we do not charge for that, and we look to be as thorough and as accurate as possible and as inclusive as possible.

I would love for— to connect with your team, because as we celebrate Ecuador, my district by far has the largest Ecuadorian population and Ecuadorian restaurants that should be featured here. And that's just one example. I wanted to dig in a little more just to get a better understanding of the Little Neighborhoods campaign,

what that looks like, how's that being promoted, how is that being explained to those neighborhoods, like, what does that look like, and what's the benefit to the little neighborhoods of that campaign?

Thank you, Council Member. So this is part of that passport really just encouraging folks to– as they're checking off cultural institutions– to consider visiting all of those neighborhoods as another type of scavenger hunt. I don't anticipate that this is going to drive tourists in the thousands to these neighborhoods or be something that would be logistically difficult for neighborhoods to absorb. So, in that capacity, I don't know that there's been specific outreach. We are in really constant conversation with BIDs, chambers. You know, to the extent that there are existing organizations for— not, not every one of those, like, designated little neighborhoods has an association to work with, but where there is, the Passport team will be in touch with them.

I just wanted to clarify one thing. The team-specific landing pages on our website are not yet live. So if you have additional input on Ecuador-specific

businesses, we'd love to talk to you because we're building all that now.
Absolutely. Ask one last question. We're less than two months away. There's a lot of building, a lot of development. Are we ready for this?
Yes.
Okay.

Alright, we're ready. I wanted to touch on Sean– Majority Leader Abreu's bills on bathrooms. So the first set of questions, just the, the assessment of where we are currently, how many public bathrooms are open and operational in the areas where we expect increased traffic, so those five fan zones, and what's the state of play at the moment?

Okay. With regard to the fan zones, again, those are operated by the New York-New Jersey host committee in conjunction with partners similar like Tishman Speyer or Adidas. And for— they are kind of managed like we would manage any other large-scale event that we would host in New York City, meaning that the event organizers work with us to ensure that they are providing the

appropriate number of restrooms per number of guests and ensure that the number, at least five of those, are accessible. So, they will be providing additional restrooms in those areas to ensure that they are complying with all city, state, and federal regulations.

Yeah, hi. And from Parks' perspective, we'll just add, as we mentioned in our testimony, you know, we have— we were proud to offer well over 700 public restroom buildings, all throughout the city, some of which, you know, certainly overlap with areas that we can anticipate will be, you know, quite busy this summer, as they are every summer, but certainly with all the exciting events going on this year.
And does the Parks Department anticipate you'll need additional funding to cover the cost of maintaining bathrooms or increased usage?

We appreciate the question very much, and we're proud to say that, you know, obviously New York's keeping our restroom facilities, you know, clean and usable in a good condition is a top priority of the agency, and we always do that

with the resources that are available. We're in ongoing conversations with the Mayor's Office and OMB, as you know, it's a consistent dialogue, but we're, you know, we're confident that we're up to the task. And, you know, frankly, every summer is very, very busy here in New York City. I think there's a lot of ways in which this summer will be unique for sure, but there are other ways in which not quite so much, right? This is something we're really quite used to. So we're in the midst of staffing up thousands employees as part of our seasonal plan. We bring on an additional couple thousand individuals through our Parks Opportunity Program. So we're staffing up as we do every summer. That's for our beaches, our pools, our parks, our playgrounds, recreational playground associates, security staff in the form of city seasonal aides. So it's a very robust staffing expansion that happens every summer, and this summer we're obviously taking a keen look at the resources that are on hand and we're continuing those conversations.

And have you coordinated with the czar's office on community

soccer programming or any open play opportunities that you plan to have in New York City parks?

Soccer or football as it's called by others, is obviously a beloved sport by New Yorkers all over the city. I– you know, we're proud of our soccer fields and they're count— excuse me, countless number of groups that keep those, you know, fields activated and active. We have an athletic permit site on our– that features an interactive map so you can sort of see what fields are available for pickup games. It's obviously hugely popular. There's also structured play that takes place with permit— excuse me, athletic permit through leagues or what have you for youth and adults alike.
Is there a plan to expand in connection with the World Cup? And if so, by how much?

So the existing facilities that are the existing facilities, so I don't know about expand, but obviously we are doing everything in our power to draw attention to and highlight and accentuate, you know, the availability of these fields, and because we want New Yorkers and visitors, you know, out there enjoying these spaces.

And just back to the other question, understanding that the fan zones are operated separately, but do we have a sense of what the current situation is of public restrooms if we weren't to invest further? Like the snapshot now of whether or not we have enough capacity and where we need more.

It is my understanding that as we're still under development of the plans, but that there will be the appropriate number of restrooms available per the expected number of guests coming into those areas.
And do we know the current hours of those existing facilities and if they're– they would need to be extended during the tournament?
Well, they would be specific to those tournament spaces. So they would probably– they would align with the tournament, with the hours of operations of those sites.
And is there a plan for temporary restrooms as well?

That is a temporary restroom, because– well, for example, the

tennis center, obviously that's fine on its own. But spaces like Brooklyn Bridge Park, there would need to be temporary restrooms associated with that event. Tishman Speyer, I'm not sure where we have landed with that, but if temporary restrooms are required, then we would ensure that they are put in place in those locations to accommodate the influx in the number of guests coming into that area.
Great. And do we have an analysis of existing restroom capacity against what we expect in terms of daily attendance in the fan zones to identify that delta?
We do not have that. So that is something that we can look at for you.
Or I imagine would be part of the plan coming in.
It is part of the plan.
In June 1st. And just to– for the record, which agency is going to be responsible for delivering the plan?

You know, if I could just speak from Parks' perspective, I think, you know,

our– as I think all the groups you've heard today, all the offices and entities, I think, you know, planning, is underway. You know, if the question is, will there be a binder, you know, with plan on the cover of it, that I think will take a little more discussion in terms of the— I think we're open to working with the sponsor of the legislation to kind of work through what that really looks like. I think what we're hearing today is that, you know, we all support the intent of this bill, and you know, the entities, the city is planning, preparing, this is all underway. Whether that results in some sort of work product or document is maybe a different– slightly different question that, you know, I think we're engaged with the sponsor on.

The most important document would be that to the public so that the public are aware of where these facilities are. And I guess another question on this plan, but the standards for cleanliness, maintenance, and staffing during the World Cup, if there's an agency responsible for cleaning, and yeah, how we would coordinate with businesses, transit hubs, cultural

institutions that are near the fan zones to help increase the capacity around this influx of activity.

I think if you're characterizing the overall sort of cleanliness of, say, city streetway, you know, street corridors, that kind of thing, we're– you know, we're happy to consult with our our agency partners at DSNY to kind of have that discussion. Speaking from Parks' perspective, if there is a special event being planned, those event organizers are generally tasked, you know, with a plan to make sure that the– you know, that the park in this case is, you know, is kept clean or that resources are provided so that it can be sort of returned, you know, to normal as was– as would be expected. And I believe that's also the case for street events or what have you.

That is correct. The event organizers are responsible and must have sanitation and cleanup plans for any of their activities. It's a requirement for the permit. So when we're looking at restrooms and cleanliness and stuff like that, that is a part of their permit requirements to provide the appropriate number of restrooms for their event and to ensure that they're

maintained and cleaned. And also to ensure on a general sense, it's not just the restrooms alone, that the areas that they're occupying are maintained and clean at all times.
Understood.
And we also coordinate with sanitation to ensure that they are working directly with them.

I'm referring to these five fan zones, where we need to see a little bit more of a plan for the capacity. I want to acknowledge that Council Member Brewer has joined us, and give her the opportunity to ask questions.

Thank you. Thank you very much. I– Council Member may have already asked. Obviously, we have lots of people who want to have events related and not related, literally even if you're just a block association that hasn't had a block association event in the past, the answer is no during this time. Is that a correct statement?

The answer is that we're going to review your application and ensure as long as those resources are available to host the event, it can move forward. If there are not

resources available to host the event, then we can't move forward.
Okay, so it's case by case is what you're saying?
Correct. Like, we, as you know, we get lots and lots of applications in. We do again have our policy and in our rules that the events that take place in the previous year have the right to—
[interposing] No, and that's why I made very clear, said it would be a new event.
So all new events are being analyzed and assessed based on resources and other things, and they have input from other agencies as to whether they may be able to move forward or not.

Okay. Second question is– it's– I guess that would apply— in other words, if a bar is having an event, that would not necessarily involve the street, but it might, because everybody's going to want do something that is not— people can't get the tickets to go, they may or may not go to Rockefeller Center if they live in

Manhattan, unless the event there. So, do you need— are they going to need extra information if people spill out into the street? Is there any other kind of way that people can see the programs other than Rockefeller Center, going to the Meadowlands, etcetera? How else are people going to participate? What's your envision for that?
Hi, Council Member. Good to see you. Great question. We anticipate that there will be all kinds of places to view the game. So the Fan Fest will certainly be a place where—
[interposing] That we know—
free viewing.
Right.

In addition, I think over the course of the next month, we'll— more and more events will be announced and stood up from parks to plazas. We know that everyone is well aware of the permit restrictions that have been in place, and part of that was so some of this programming could be stood up. In addition, the

portal that New York City Tourism is hosting will be a place where entities can list their viewing parties. So we know that museums, all kinds of institutions are planning on hosting viewings. ABNY just released a list of their grantees. A lot of those events and activations are for viewing parties. So, I think–
